title: The Widow's Gift and the Coming Destruction

verses.text: Then Jesus looked up and saw the rich putting their gifts into the treasury,
and He saw a poor widow put in two small copper coins.
"Truly I tell you," He said, "this poor widow has put in more than all the others.
For they all contributed out of their surplus, but she out of her poverty has put in all she had to live on."
As some of the disciples were remarking how the temple was adorned with beautiful stones and consecrated gifts, Jesus said,
"As for what you see here, the time will come when not one stone will be left on another; every one will be thrown down."
"Teacher," they asked, "when will these things happen? And what will be the sign that they are about to take place?"
Jesus answered, "See to it that you are not deceived. For many will come in My name, claiming, 'I am He,' and, 'The time is near.' Do not follow them.
When you hear of wars and rebellions, do not be alarmed. These things must happen first, but the end is not imminent."
Then He told them, "Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom.
There will be great earthquakes, famines, and pestilences in various places, along with fearful sights and great signs from heaven.
But before all this, they will seize you and persecute you. On account of My name they will deliver you to the synagogues and prisons, and they will bring you before kings and governors.
This will be your opportunity to serve as witnesses.
So make up your mind not to worry beforehand how to defend yourselves.
For I will give you speech and wisdom that none of your adversaries will be able to resist or contradict.
You will be betrayed even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends, and some of you will be put to death.
And you will be hated by everyone because of My name.
Yet not even a hair of your head will perish.
By your patient endurance you will gain your souls.
But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, you will know that her desolation is near.
Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, let those in the city get out, and let those in the country stay out of the city.
For these are the days of vengeance, to fulfill all that is written.
How miserable those days will be for pregnant and nursing mothers! For there will be great distress upon the land and wrath against this people.
They will fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive into all the nations. And Jerusalem will be trodden down by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.
There will be signs in the sun and moon and stars, and on the earth dismay among the nations, bewildered by the roaring of the sea and the surging of the waves.
Men will faint from fear and anxiety over what is coming upon the earth, for the powers of the heavens will be shaken.
At that time they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory.
When these things begin to happen, stand up and lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near."
Then Jesus told them a parable: "Look at the fig tree and all the trees.
When they sprout leaves, you can see for yourselves and know that summer is near.
So also, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near.
Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened.
Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away.
But watch yourselves, or your hearts will be weighed down by dissipation, drunkenness, and the worries of life—and that day will spring upon you suddenly like a snare.
For it will come upon all who dwell on the face of all the earth.
So keep watch at all times, and pray that you may have the strength to escape all that is about to happen and to stand before the Son of Man."
Every day Jesus taught at the temple, but every evening He went out to spend the night on the Mount of Olives.
And early in the morning all the people would come to hear Him at the temple.

context.author: Luke, the physician and companion of Paul
context.genre: Apocalyptic discourse: a short narrative of a widow's gift, followed by Jesus' teaching on the temple's fall, the end of the age, and the return of the Son of Man
context.audience: The disciples, who were admiring the temple (v.5), with the people nearby. Luke's Gentile readers, writing before or after Jerusalem's fall, are told how to watch and when to flee.
context.mapLabel: THE TEMPLE AND THE MOUNT OF OLIVES
context.setting: Jesus is still in the temple courts and sits near the treasury, where thirteen trumpet-shaped chests received offerings. The temple, rebuilt by Herod the Great, was one of the great buildings of the ancient world, with stones some of which measured over thirty feet. At night He leaves for the Mount of Olives (v.37), from where the temple stands in full view.
context.custom: Two small copper coins, the lepta, were the smallest coin in circulation and worth a small fraction of a day's wage. The wealthy often dropped large coins noisily into the trumpet-shaped receptacles, so the giving was public. Many in Jesus' time expected a Messiah to rescue Jerusalem and punish Rome, so His statement that the temple would be thrown down was shocking to the listeners.
context.timelineImmediate: After the last controversy in chapter 20, Jesus watches a widow give and then, at the disciples' admiration of the temple, speaks about its fall. Chapter 22 begins the Passover week proper, with the plot against Jesus, the Last Supper, and the arrest.
context.timelineBible: The language of earthquakes, signs in the heavens, and the Son of Man coming in a cloud draws on Daniel 7:13-14 and Joel 2:30-31. The desolation of Jerusalem has precedent in Jeremiah 52 and the Babylonian siege. The "times of the Gentiles" in verse 24 adds a period of foreign rule over the city before the Son of Man returns.
context.sparkNotes: Jesus watches the rich put gifts into the treasury and praises a poor widow who gave two small coins, because she gave all she had. When the disciples admire the temple, He says every stone will be thrown down. Asked when this will happen, He warns of deception, wars, earthquakes, and persecution, and promises words and wisdom for those who must testify. He describes Jerusalem surrounded by armies and tells those in Judea to flee, then speaks of signs in the heavens and the Son of Man coming in a cloud with great glory. He ends with the lesson of the fig tree and a call to keep watch and pray.

translation.meaning: Lack or shortage. The widow gave out of her need, while the others gave out of their surplus (perisseuontōn, "overflow"). Jesus measures giving by what is left, not by what is given.
Encircled, as in a siege. Luke adds this detail to the saying about the "abomination of desolation" in Mark and Matthew and makes it concrete: Jerusalem encircled by armies.
A period during which the nations tread down Jerusalem. Readers differ on its length and meaning, but Jesus speaks of it as a fixed span with an end.
Release by payment of a ransom. In the middle of the terror Jesus tells His followers to lift up their heads because their final release is near.

commentary.note: Henry sees the widow's gift as proof that "charity to the poor is a main matter in religion." Christ notices both how much we give and how willingly we give, and He values her small gift above the rich men's larger ones. On the temple, he says outward splendor is fragile and calls a preoccupation with a church's "pomps" "a poor thing" compared with God's presence and ordinances. On persecution, he warns that "nothing introduces a surer or sorer ruin than the sin of persecution."

Henry says Jesus uses the imagery of sun, moon, and stars as figures for the fall of Jerusalem, and that the same language points ahead to the last day and the terror it brings to people without faith. On the fig tree, he says we read the signs of the times as we read the budding of trees: when the causes appear, so does the advance of God's judgments and kingdom. He urges constant watchfulness and prayer, and says those who "live a life of prayer in this world" will be counted worthy to praise God in the next.

Gill says the widow gave "all the living she had" and values her gift by her ability to give, not its amount, so she gave more than the rich. He reads the armies of verse 20 as the Roman forces under Titus, and says that once the city was besieged its destruction was near and no deliverance was to be expected. On the closing warning, he urges believers to guard against every sin, especially overindulgence and worldly cares, and to pray continually, and says they will be counted worthy "through the grace and goodness of God," not through their own watchfulness.

Lewis does not comment on Luke 21 by verse, but his essay "The World's Last Night" takes up the saying in verse 32 that "this generation will not pass away." He treats it candidly as a hard saying that Christians cannot ignore. He sets it beside Jesus' admission in Mark 13:32 that He does not know the day or hour, and he concludes that we should neither predict the date nor stop expecting the return. (Paraphrased; Lewis's works remain under copyright.)

overview.summary: Jesus praises a poor widow's small gift, then tells His disciples the temple will be torn down. He warns of deception, wars, persecution, and Jerusalem surrounded by armies, and urges them to stay alert and pray.
overview.settingLine: The temple courts, then the Mount of Olives.

history.t: Herod's rebuilt temple was a wonder of the world, which makes the prediction shocking.
Rome destroyed Jerusalem and the temple in AD 70, about forty years later.

customs.t: Thirteen trumpet-shaped chests held offerings, so large gifts were heard dropping in.
Two lepta were the smallest coins, worth a tiny fraction of a day's wage.

archaeology.t: Huge stones thrown down from the temple walls in AD 70 still lie where they fell.
Tiny bronze lepta have been found in Jerusalem, many no bigger than a fingernail.

overview.discussion: Jesus praised the widow's two coins over the large gifts. How do you measure generosity?
overview.book: The third Gospel · 24 chapters. Written as an orderly account, with Acts as its sequel.
overview.author: Luke
overview.audience: Theophilus and a broad, largely Gentile readership
